name: Rafael Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rafael, 27. I'm assistant stockman on the home farm at the Ardmore estate, about 200 beef cattle, a flock of sheep, and a lot of grass we cut for silage and hay. I've been there just over two years. I live with Nina, who teaches at the primary school in the village, and my grandad left me a small flat in town that I rent out, so money's not the worry it is for some. I don't post online and I don't use AI, never have.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, feed round with the tractor and the diet feeder, then checking the cattle in the sheds and the ones out on the hill. Gordon, the head stockman, does the clever stuff like calving problems and vet calls, and I'm still learning that. In summer it's silage and baling, long days in the cab. I like being out on the hill first thing, when it's just you and the cattle. What wears me out is the estate office sending emails about spreadsheets and ear-tag records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, I'm not a big talker about this stuff. If it came up in the pub, I'd say it's like most new things, some of it useful, a lot of noise. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think good, carry on. My job is cattle and grass, and a computer program isn't going to drive a feeder wagon. I'd be glad to keep my head down and learn the job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep learning off Gordon, get better at calving, maybe do the sheep-shearing course in spring. Keep the rent from the flat going into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing happened, which is how I'd like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. In this picture, does anyone at Ardmore try to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate office, maybe. They'd want ear-tag records done on some app instead of paper. I'd let Gordon deal with it, or I'd do it slowly and complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want from the next few years if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be good at this. In five years I want Gordon to go on holiday and not ring me every day. That's the whole plan, really.

S0.say: He'd say it's like most new things, some of it useful and a lot of noise. He wouldn't say much more, and he doesn't post online.
S0.think: Privately he'd be glad, because his job is cattle and grass, not computer programs. He'd keep his head down and learn the job properly.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, learns calving from the head stockman and signs up for a sheep-shearing course in spring. Keeps putting the rent from his flat into savings.
S0.feel: Calm, as if nothing happened, which is how he'd like it.
S0.quote: In five years I want Gordon to go on holiday and not ring me every day. That's the whole plan, really.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is quiet, practical and doesn't take sides on the big questions. His goal is modest and concrete: to be trusted alone with the herd. The rented flat gives him a calm baseline that shapes how he answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms have always changed, tractors replaced horses and people got on with it. Some of it'll be good and some won't. I'd probably say that and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it makes me a bit nervous. The feed round is the first thing I'd expect a machine to do, and that's half my morning. Gordon's job is safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the estate brings in, and I'd keep my head down. I'd stop thinking about the new pickup I was going to buy and put that money away. If they offered training I'd go, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What on the Ardmore farm do you think changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feeding, then the silage. There's already self-driving feeder wagons, Gordon showed me a video. The estate manager loves anything that saves a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you should start learning any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, and I know that. But I'd rather wait till I see it actually working on a farm near us. I've seen too many fancy things end up rusting in the corner of a shed.

S1.say: He'd say farms have always changed, from horses to tractors, and people got on with it. Some of it would be good and some wouldn't.
S1.think: Privately he's a bit nervous, because the feed round is the first thing a machine would take and it's half his morning. He thinks the head stockman's job is safer than his.
S1.do: Waits to see what the estate brings in and keeps his head down. Shelves buying a new pickup and puts that money away, and goes on training only if it's offered.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with worry in the background but no lost sleep.
S1.quote: I've seen too many fancy things end up rusting in the corner of a shed.
S1.fieldNote: He recognises that he probably should learn the tools and chooses to wait anyway, which is his resistant streak in plain sight. His concern is specific: the feed round. He blames no one in particular, though the estate manager's love of saving wages comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, nobody's ready, and someone should slow it down. I'm not a political person, but I'd want the government to do something. I'd say it at the pub and leave the marching to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it scares me. I don't know these tools at all, I've never used one. If a robot can calve a cow and drive the feeder, I'm a stockman with nothing to stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no new truck, no holiday. I'd look for any work still needing a person, maybe hedging or fencing contracts, and I'd ask around. I'd lean on Nina's wage and the rent from the flat while I worked it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got the flat and Nina's job. Does that make this easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the bills, yes, we wouldn't go hungry. But I'm not a landlord, I'm a stockman. Living off one flat's rent isn't a life, it's waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandad, if he could hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say get your hands dirty and stop moaning. He was a builder, and he bought that flat by working Saturdays for 20 years. I think he'd be as lost as me, though.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast, nobody's ready, and someone should slow it down. He'd say it at the pub and leave the marching to others.
S2.think: Privately it scares him, because he's never used these tools. If a robot can calve a cow and drive the feeder, he's a stockman with nothing to stock.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard at once, dropping the new truck and the holiday. Looks for fencing or hedging contracts and leans on his partner's wage and the flat's rent while he works things out.
S2.feel: Scared and losing sleep, with two years feeling like nothing.
S2.quote: I'm not a landlord, I'm a stockman. Living off one flat's rent isn't a life, it's waiting.
S2.fieldNote: His money is safe, but his sense of who he is isn't, and that drives the alarm. He separates what he'd say in public from a private fear he admits plainly. His grandad, a builder who bought the flat by hard work, is clearly a model for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's something. People should get some help to change jobs. I'd say it to Gordon and Nina, mostly, not to the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably waste the first two years telling myself it's not real. That's how I am. Then I'd be in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at a hoof-trimming course, because that's still hands-on with cattle and every farm needs it. I'd keep saving the rent and cut back on the pickup again. I'd ask Gordon what he thinks, because he's seen more change than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's coming and I can see it, which helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get a trade that's mine, not the estate's. With two years I'd just be scrambling. With five I can at least learn one thing properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hoof trimming, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cattle won't stand still for a machine, not ours anyway. You need someone who can read a cow that's about to kick. I might be wrong, but it's the best bet I've got.

S3.say: He'd say five years is short but it's something, and people should get some help to change jobs. He'd say it to people he knows, not to the world.
S3.think: Privately he thinks he'd waste the first two years telling himself it's not real, because that's how he is. Then he'd be in a hurry.
S3.do: Looks into a hoof-trimming course in the first year as a hands-on trade of his own. Keeps saving the rent from his flat and holds off on the pickup again.
S3.feel: Anxious, though seeing it coming helps a bit.
S3.quote: You need someone who can read a cow that's about to kick.
S3.fieldNote: He predicts his own procrastination with real honesty. Hoof trimming is a very concrete choice that keeps him with cattle and away from screens. The extra years give him one practical step, not a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots can change. I'd say let's see. That's what most people round here would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not that bothered by it. Ten years is a lifetime in farming terms. I'll be 37, I'll know cattle properly, and I'll have the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much at first. Keep going, keep saving, keep the flat let. Maybe in five years, if it's still coming, I'd do the hoof-trimming course I talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Something to think about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound much more relaxed about this one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't do anything about something ten years off. You don't worry about next year's calving in this year's spring. I know that sounds daft after what I said before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Nina change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe buy a second flat with the savings, if prices are right. Nina wants kids at some point, and that wouldn't change. Ten years is too far to plan a life around.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so let's see. He thinks most people round there would say the same.
S4.think: Privately he's not that bothered, since ten years is a lifetime in farming terms. He'll be 37, know cattle properly and still have the flat.
S4.do: Keeps going and keeps saving with the flat let out. Considers buying a second flat if prices are right, and leaves the hoof-trimming course for five years' time.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, treating it as something for later.
S4.quote: You don't worry about next year's calving in this year's spring.
S4.fieldNote: This is the clearest example of his wait-and-see habit: the same end point feels distant and harmless with ten years. He notices his own contradiction and accepts it. His only active idea is a second flat, an asset rather than a skill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no trade except this one and no time to get another. What would help is somebody paying for a proper course, like hoof trimming or fencing, and a bit of time to do it before the job goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd miss. I'd miss the hill at six in the morning with nobody else about. You can't pay someone for that, and you can't give it to a robot either.

headlineQuote: If a robot can calve a cow and drive the feeder, I'm a stockman with nothing to stock.
portrait: Rafael Quinn is a 27-year-old assistant stockman on the Ardmore estate's beef and sheep farm, living with Nina, a primary school teacher, and owning a small rented-out flat left to him by his grandad. He's quiet, practical and in the middle on politics, and he has never used AI. His money keeps him safe, but the fast AGI picture alarms him because it takes away who he is. With five years he'd look at hoof trimming, and with ten he's calm and openly says he'd wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no trade except this one and no time to get another.
whatWouldHelp: Someone paying for a proper course, like hoof trimming or fencing, and time to do it before the job goes.
